\\\"source_original\\\", \\\"content\\\": \\\"--- PAGE 1 ---\\\\nSGLang: Efficient Execution of\\\\nStructured Language Model Programs\\\\nLianmin Zheng2∗\\\\nLiangsheng Yin3\\\\nZhiqiang Xie1\\\\nChuyue Sun1\\\\nJeff Huang4\\\\nCody Hao Yu5\\\\nShiyi Cao2\\\\nChristos Kozyrakis1\\\\nIon Stoica2\\\\nJoseph E. Gonzalez2\\\\nClark Barrett1\\\\nYing Sheng1∗\\\\n1 Stanford University\\\\n2 UC Berkeley\\\\n3 Shanghai Jiao Tong University\\\\n4 Texas A&M University\\\\n5 Independent Researcher\\\\nAbstract\\\\nLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for complex tasks that\\\\nrequire multiple generation calls, advanced prompting techniques, control flow, and\\\\nstructured inputs/outputs. However, efficient systems are lacking for programming\\\\nand executing these applications. We introduce SGLang, a system for efficient\\\\nexecution of complex language model programs. SGLang consists of a frontend\\\\nlanguage and a runtime. The frontend simplifies programming with primitives for\\\\ngeneration and parallelism control. The runtime accelerates execution with novel\\\\noptimizations like RadixAttention for KV cache reuse and compressed finite state\\\\nmachines for faster structured output decoding. Experiments show that SGLang\\\\nachieves up to 6.4× higher throughput compared to state-of-the-art inference\\\\nsystems on various large language and multi-modal models on tasks including\\\\nagent control, logical reasoning, few-shot learning benchmarks, JSON decoding,\\\\nretrieval-augmented generation pipelines, and multi-turn chat. The code is publicly\\\\navailable at https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nRecent increases in the capabilities of LLMs have broadened their utility, enabling them to tackle a\\\\nwider range of general tasks and act as autonomous agents [35, 6, 36, 52, 46]. In such applications,\\\\nLLMs engage in multi-round planning, reasoning, and interaction with external environments. This\\\\nis accomplished through tool usage [41, 38], multiple input modalities [47, 2], and a wide range of\\\\nprompting techniques [30], like few-shot learning [5], self-consistency [53], skeleton-of-thought [33],\\\\nand tree-of-thought [56]. All of these new use cases require multiple, often dependent, LLM\\\\ngeneration calls, showing a trend of using multi-call structures to complete complex tasks [57, 21].\\\\nThe emergence of these patterns signifies a shift in our interaction with LLMs, moving from simple\\\\nchatting to a more sophisticated form of programmatic usage of LLMs, which means using a program\\\\nto schedule and control the generation processes of LLMs. We refer to these programs as \\\\\\\"Language\\\\nModel Programs\\\\\\\" (LM Programs) [4, 20]. The advanced prompting techniques and agentic workflow\\\\nmentioned above fall within the scope of LM programs. There are two common properties of LM\\\\nprograms: (1) LM programs typically contain multiple LLM calls interspersed with control flow.\\\\nThis is needed to complete complex tasks and improve overall quality. (2) LM programs receive\\\\nstructured inputs and produce structured outputs. This is needed to enable the composition of LM\\\\nprograms and to integrate LM programs into existing software systems.\\\\n∗Equal contribution.\\\\nPreprint. Under review.\\\\narXiv:2312.07104v2  [cs.AI]  6 Jun 2024\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 2 ---\\\\nInterpreter\\\\nSGLang Client (Frontend)\\\\nLanguage primitives (Sec. 2)\\\\nSGLang Runtime (Backend)\\\\nOptimizations: RadixAttention (Sec. 3), Compressed finite \\\\nstate machines (Sec. 4), API speculative execution (Sec. 5)\\\\nFigure 1: System architecture: An interpreter executes language primitives with optimized runtime.\\\\nDespite the widespread use of LM programs, current systems for expressing and executing them\\\\nremain inefficient. We identify two primary challenges associated with the efficient use of LM pro-\\\\ngrams: First, programming LM programs is tedious and difficult due to the non-deterministic nature of\\\\nLLMs. Developing an LM program often requires extensive string manipulation, experimental tuning\\\\nof prompts, brittle output parsing, handling multiple input modalities, and implementing parallelism\\\\nmechanisms. This complexity significantly reduces the readability of even simple programs (Sec. 2).\\\\nSecondly and importantly, executing LM programs is inefficient due to redundant computation\\\\nand memory usage. State-of-the-art inference engines (e.g., vLLM [23], TGI [16], and TensorRT-\\\\nLLM [34]), have been optimized to reduce latency and improve throughput without direct knowledge\\\\nof the workload. This makes these systems general and robust but also results in significant ineffi-\\\\nciencies for any given workload. A prominent example is the reuse of the Key-Value (KV) cache\\\\n(Sec. 3). The KV cache consists of reusable intermediate tensors that are essential for generative\\\\ninference. During typical batch executions of LM programs, numerous opportunities exist to reuse\\\\nthe KV cache across multiple different LLM calls that share a common prefix. However, current\\\\nsystems lack effective mechanisms to facilitate this reuse, resulting in unnecessary computations and\\\\nwasted memory. Another example is constrained decoding for structured outputs (e.g., JSON mode),\\\\nwhere the output of LLMs is restricted to follow specific grammatical rules defined by a regular\\\\nexpression (Sec. 4). Under these constraints, multiple tokens can often be decoded once. However,\\\\nexisting systems only decode one token at a time, leading to suboptimal decoding speeds.\\\\nTo address these challenges, we present SGLang, a Structured Generation Language for LLMs. The\\\\ncore idea is to systematically exploit the multi-call structure in LM programs for efficient execution.\\\\nAs shown in Fig. 1, it has two parts: a front-end language and a back-end runtime. The front-end\\\\nsimplifies the programming of LM programs, and the runtime accelerates their execution. The two\\\\nparts can work together for better performance but can also function independently.\\\\nWe introduce SGLang as a domain-specific language embedded in Python. It provides primitives\\\\nfor generation (e.g., extend, gen, select) and parallelism control (e.g., fork, join). SGLang\\\\nis compatible with Python’s control flow and libraries, so users can develop advanced prompting\\\\nworkflows easily with native Python syntax. We provide an interpreter and a compiler for SGLang.\\\\nThe interpreter manages the prompt state as a stream and submits primitive operations to the stream for\\\\nasynchronous execution, ensuring proper control over synchronization and intra-program parallelism.\\\\nAdditionally, SGLang program can be traced and compiled for more optimizations.\\\\nOn the runtime side, we propose several novel optimizations to accelerate the execution of SGLang\\\\nprograms. The first technique, RadixAttention, enables the automatic reuse of the KV cache across\\\\nmultiple generation calls. In existing inference engines, the KV cache of a request is discarded\\\\nafter processing is completed, preventing the KV cache from being reused across multiple calls and\\\\nsignificantly slowing down the execution. Instead, our system maintains an LRU cache of the KV\\\\ncache for all requests within a radix tree. This approach manages the KV cache as a traditional cache\\\\nand uses a radix tree for efficient matching, insertion, and eviction. It allows the runtime to handle\\\\nvarious reuse patterns with a cache-aware scheduling policy efficiently. The second technique is a\\\\ncompressed finite state machine, which enables faster constrained decoding for structured outputs.\\\\nExisting systems follow the constraints only for the next token by masking probabilities of disallowed\\\\ntokens, making them able to decode only one token at a time. Instead, our system analyzes the\\\\nconstraints and builds a compressed finite-state machine to represent the constraint. This approach\\\\ncompresses a multi-token path into a single-step path whenever possible, allowing the decoding of\\\\nmultiple tokens at once to achieve faster decoding speed. Lastly, SGLang also supports API-only\\\\nmodels like OpenAI’s GPT-4, and we introduce the third technique, API speculative execution, to\\\\noptimize multi-call programs for API-only models.\\\\nUsing SGLang, we implemented various LLM applications, including agent control, logical reasoning,\\\\nfew-shot learning benchmarks, JSON decoding, retrieval-augmented generation pipelines, multi-\\\\nturn chat, and multi-modality processing. We tested the performance on models including Llama-\\\\n7B/70B [49], Mistral-8x7B [17], LLaVA-v1.5-7B (image) [28], and LLaVA-NeXT-34B (video) [62]\\\\non NVIDIA A10G and A100 GPUs. Experimental results show that SGLang achieves up to 6.4×\\\\nhigher throughput across a wide range of workloads, models, and hardware setups, compared to\\\\nexisting programming and inference systems, including Guidance [13], vLLM [23], and LMQL [4].\\\\n2\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\ndimensions = [\\\\\\\"Clarity\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"Originality\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"Evidence\\\\\\\"]\\\\n@function\\\\ndef multi_dimensional_judge(s, path, essay): \\\\ns += system(\\\\\\\"Evaluate an essay about an image.\\\\\\\")\\\\ns += user(image(path) + \\\\\\\"Essay:\\\\\\\" + essay)\\\\ns += assistant(\\\\\\\"Sure!\\\\\\\")\\\\n# Return directly if it is not related\\\\ns += user(\\\\\\\"Is the essay related to the image?\\\\\\\")\\\\ns += assistant(select(\\\\\\\"related\\\\\\\", choices=[\\\\\\\"yes\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"no\\\\\\\"]))\\\\nif s[\\\\\\\"related\\\\\\\"] == \\\\\\\"no\\\\\\\": return\\\\n# Judge multiple dimensions in parallel\\\\nforks = s.fork(len(dimensions))\\\\nfor f, dim in zip(forks, dimensions):\\\\nf += user(\\\\\\\"Evaluate based on the following dimension:\\\\\\\" +\\\\ndim + \\\\\\\". Primitives provided by SGLang are shown in red.\\\\n2\\\\nProgramming Model\\\\nThis section introduces the SGLang programming model with a running example, describes its\\\\nlanguage primitives and execution modes, and outlines runtime optimization opportunities. This\\\\nprogramming model can simplify tedious operations in multi-call workflows (e.g., string manipulation,\\\\nAPI calling, constraint specification, parallelism) by providing flexible and composable primitives.\\\\nA running example. The language is a domain-specific language embedded in Python. Fig. 2 shows a\\\\nprogram that evaluates an essay about an image using the branch-solve-merge prompting method [40].\\\\nThe function multi_dimensional_judge takes three arguments: s, path, and essay. s manages\\\\nthe prompt state, path is the image file path, and essay is the essay text. New strings and SGLang\\\\nprimitives can be appended to the state s for execution using the += operator. First, the function\\\\nadds the image and essay to the prompt. It then checks if the essay is related to the image using\\\\nselect, storing the result in s[\\\\\\\"related\\\\\\\"]. If related, the prompt is forked into three copies for\\\\nparallel evaluation from different dimensions, using gen to store results in f[\\\\\\\"judgment\\\\\\\"]. Next, it\\\\nmerges the judgments, generates a summary, and assigns a letter grade. Finally, it returns the results\\\\nin JSON format, following a schema defined by a regular expression constraint regex. SGLang\\\\ngreatly simplifies this program, as an equivalent program using an OpenAI API-like interface would\\\\ntake 2.1× as many lines of code due to manual string manipulation and parallelism control.\\\\nLanguage primitives. SGLang provides primitives for controlling prompt state, generation, and\\\\nparallelism. They can be used together with Python syntax and libraries. Here are the primitives:\\\\n“gen” calls a model to generate and stores the results in a variable with the name specified in its first\\\\nargument. It supports a “regex” argument to constrain the output to follow a grammar defined by a\\\\nregular expression (e.g., a JSON schema). “select” calls a model to choose the highest probability\\\\noption from a list. The operator “+=” or “extend” appends a string to the prompt. The operator\\\\n“[variable_name]” fetches the results of a generation. “fork” creates parallel forks of the prompt\\\\nstate. “join” rejoins the prompt state. “image” and “video” take in image and video inputs.\\\\nExecution modes. The simplest way to execute an SGLang program is through an interpreter, where a\\\\nprompt is treated as an asynchronous stream. Primitives like extend, gen, and select are submitted\\\\nto the stream for asynchronous execution. These non-blocking calls allow Python code to continue\\\\nrunning without waiting for the generation to finish. This is similar to launching CUDA kernels\\\\nasynchronously. Each prompt is managed by a stream executor in a background thread, enabling\\\\nintra-program parallelism. Fetching generation results will block until they are ready, ensuring correct\\\\nsynchronization. Alternatively, SGLang programs can be compiled as computational graphs and\\\\n3\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 4 ---\\\\nTable 1: Comparison among LMQL, Guidance, and SGLang.\\\\nSystem\\\\nSyntax\\\\nLanguage Primitives\\\\nRuntime Backends\\\\nLMQL\\\\nCustom\\\\nextend, gen, select\\\\nHF Transformers, llama.cpp, OpenAI\\\\nGuidance\\\\nPython\\\\nextend, gen, select, image\\\\nHF Transformers, llama.cpp, OpenAI\\\\nSGLang\\\\nPython\\\\nextend, gen, select, image, video, fork, join\\\\nSGLang Runtime (SRT), OpenAI\\\\nexecuted with a graph executor, allowing for more optimizations. This paper uses interpreter mode by\\\\ndefault and discusses compiler mode results in Appendix D. SGLang supports open-weight models\\\\nwith its own SGLang Runtime (SRT), as well as API models such as OpenAI and Anthropic models.\\\\nComparison. Programming systems for LLMs can be classified as high-level (e.g., LangChain,\\\\nDSPy) and low-level (e.g., LMQL, Guidance, SGLang). High-level systems provide predefined or\\\\nauto-generated prompts, such as DSPy’s prompt optimizer. Low-level systems typically do not alter\\\\nprompts but allow direct manipulation of prompts and primitives. SGLang is a low-level system\\\\nsimilar to LMQL and Guidance. Table 1 compares their features. SGLang focuses more on runtime\\\\nefficiency and comes with its own co-designed runtime, allowing for novel optimizations introduced\\\\nlater. High-level languages (e.g., DSPy) can be compiled to low-level languages (e.g., SGLang). We\\\\ndemonstrate the integration of SGLang as a backend in DSPy for better runtime efficiency in Sec. 6.\\\\nRuntime optimizations. Fig. 2 shows three runtime optimization opportunities: KV cache reuse,\\\\nfast constrained decoding, API speculative execution. We will discuss them in the following sections.\\\\n3\\\\nEfficient KV Cache Reuse with RadixAttention\\\\nSGLang programs can chain multiple generation calls and create parallel copies with the \\\\\\\"fork\\\\\\\"\\\\nprimitive. Additionally, different program instances often share some common parts (e.g., system\\\\nprompts). These scenarios create many shared prompt prefixes during execution, leading to numerous\\\\nopportunities for reusing the KV cache. During LLM inference, the KV cache stores intermediate\\\\ntensors from the forward pass, reused for decoding future tokens. They are named after key-value\\\\npairs in the self-attention mechanism [51]. KV cache computation depends only on prefix tokens.\\\\nTherefore, requests with the same prompt prefix can reuse the KV cache, reducing redundant\\\\ncomputation and memory usage. More background and some examples are provided in Appendix A.\\\\nGiven the KV cache reuse opportunity, a key challenge in optimizing SGLang programs is reusing the\\\\nKV cache across multiple calls and instances. While some systems explore certain KV cache reuse\\\\ncases [23, 58, 18, 12], they often need manual configurations and cannot handle all reuse patterns\\\\n(e.g., dynamic tree structures). Consequently, most state-of-the-art inference systems recompute the\\\\nKV cache for each request. We will discuss their limitations and our differences in Sec. 7.\\\\nThis section introduces RadixAttention, a novel technique for automatic and systematic KV cache\\\\nreuse during runtime. Unlike existing systems that discard the KV cache after a generation request\\\\nfinishes, our system retains the cache for prompts and generation results in a radix tree, enabling\\\\nefficient prefix search, reuse, insertion, and eviction. We implement an LRU eviction policy and\\\\na cache-aware scheduling policy to enhance the cache hit rate. RadixAttention is compatible with\\\\ntechniques like continuous batching [60], paged attention [23], and tensor parallelism [44]. In\\\\naddition, it introduces only negligible memory and time overhead when there is no cache hit.\\\\nRadixAttention. A radix tree is a data structure that serves as a space-efficient alternative to a\\\\nclassical trie (prefix tree). Unlike typical trees, the edges of a radix tree can be labeled not just\\\\nwith single elements but also with sequences of elements of varying lengths, significantly enhancing\\\\nefficiency. In our system, we utilize a radix tree to manage a mapping between sequences of tokens,\\\\nand their corresponding KV cache tensors. These KV cache tensors are stored in a non-contiguous,\\\\npaged layout, where the size of each page is equivalent to one token. Because GPU memory is quickly\\\\nfilled by the KV cahce, we introduce a simple LRU eviction policy that evicts the least recently\\\\nused leaf first. By evicting leaves first, we enable the re-use of their common ancestors until those\\\\nancestors become leaves and are also evicted.\\\\nIn the continuous batching setting, we cannot evict nodes used by the currently running batch.\\\\nTherefore, each node maintains a reference counter indicating how many running requests are using\\\\nit. A node is evictable if its reference counter is zero. Note that we do not preallocate a fixed-size\\\\nmemory pool as a cache. Instead, we let the cached tokens and the currently running requests share\\\\nthe same memory pool. Therefore, the system dynamically allocates memory for cache and running\\\\nrequests. When enough waiting requests run, the system will evict all cached tokens in favor of a\\\\nlarger batch size. Fig. 3 shows how the radix tree is maintained for several incoming requests. The new turn is appended to the\\\\ntree as a new node. In step (4), a new chat session begins. The node “b” from (3) is split into two\\\\nnodes to allow the two chat sessions to share the system prompt. In step (5), the second chat session\\\\ncontinues. However, due to the memory limit, node \\\\\\\"c\\\\\\\" from (4) must be evicted. The new turn is\\\\nappended after node \\\\\\\"d\\\\\\\" in (4). In step (6), the server receives a few-shot learning query, processes it,\\\\nand inserts it into the tree. The root node is split because the new query does not share any prefix with\\\\nexisting nodes. In step (7), the server receives a batch of additional few-shot learning queries. These\\\\nqueries share the same set of few-shot examples, so we split node ’e’ from (6) to enable sharing. In\\\\nstep (8), the server receives a new message from the first chat session. It evicts all nodes from the\\\\nsecond chat session (node \\\\\\\"g\\\\\\\" and \\\\\\\"h\\\\\\\") as they are least recently used. In step (9), the server receives\\\\na request to sample more answers for the questions in node \\\\\\\"j\\\\\\\" from (8), likely for self-consistency\\\\nprompting. To make space for these requests, we evict node \\\\\\\"i\\\\\\\", \\\\\\\"k\\\\\\\", and \\\\\\\"l\\\\\\\" in (8).\\\\nfrontend interpreter sends full prompts to the runtime, and the runtime performs prefix matching and\\\\nreuse. The tree structure is stored on the CPU with negligible maintenance overhead. During the\\\\nexecution of the fork primitive, the frontend sends the prefix first as a hint, ensuring the prefix is\\\\ncorrectly inserted into the tree. It then sends the remaining prompts. This \\\\\\\"Frontend Hint\\\\\\\" simplifies\\\\nruntime scheduling and matching, exemplifying the benefits of frontend-runtime co-design.\\\\nCache-aware scheduling. We define the cache hit rate as number of cached prompt tokens\\\\nnumber of prompt tokens\\\\n. When there are\\\\nmany requests in the waiting queue, the order in which they are executed can significantly impact\\\\nthe cache hit rate. For example, if the request scheduler frequently switches between different,\\\\nunrelated requests, it can lead to cache thrashing and a low hit rate. We design a cache-aware\\\\nscheduling algorithm to increase the cache hit rate. In the batch-processing setting we sort the\\\\n5\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 6 ---\\\\nFSM state\\\\nToken\\\\nLLM decode\\\\n(c) Decoding process with normal FSM\\\\n(d) Decoding process with compressed FSM\\\\n(a) Normal FSM for regex {\\\\\\\"summary\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"\\\\n1\\\\n{\\\\\\\"summary\\\\\\\":  \\\\\\\"\\\\n0\\\\n(b) Compressed FSM for regex {\\\\\\\"summary\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\"\\\\n{\\\\\\\"\\\\nsummary\\\\nLLM\\\\n\\\\\\\":\\\\nLLM\\\\nLLM\\\\n_\\\\\\\"\\\\nLLM\\\\nLLM\\\\n{\\\\\\\"\\\\nsummary\\\\n\\\\\\\":\\\\n_\\\\\\\"\\\\n1\\\\n2\\\\n3\\\\n5\\\\n4\\\\n6\\\\n7\\\\n8\\\\n10\\\\n9\\\\n11\\\\n{\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\ns\\\\nu\\\\nm\\\\nm\\\\na\\\\nr\\\\ny\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n:\\\\n0\\\\n12\\\\n13\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n_\\\\nFigure 4: The decoding process of normal and compressed FSMs (the underscore _ means a space).\\\\nrequests by matched prefix length and prioritize requests with longer matched prefixes instead of\\\\nusing a first-come, first-served schedule. Alg. 1 (Appendix) shows the pseudo-code for cache-aware\\\\nscheduling with contiguous batching. The algorithm uses longest-shared-prefix-first order. In more\\\\nlatency-sensitive settings we may still be able to tolerate limited batch re-ordering to improve cache\\\\nreuse. Additionally, we prove the following theorem for optimal scheduling in the offline case. 2\\\\nTheorem 3.1. For a batch of requests, we can achieve an optimal cache hit rate by visiting the radix\\\\ntree of the requests in the depth-first search order, with a cache size ≥the maximum request length.\\\\nThe longest-shared-prefix-first order is equivalent to a depth-first search order.\\\\nThe proof is in Sec. A.3 (Appendix). In the online case, the DFS order will be disrupted, but\\\\nour schedule still approximates the DFS behavior on the augmented part of the full radix tree, as\\\\ndescribed in Sec. A.3. While greedy cache-aware scheduling can achieve high throughput, it can lead\\\\nto starvation. We leave its integration with other fair scheduling methods [42] as future work.\\\\nDistributed Cases. RadixAttention can be extended to multiple GPUs. For tensor parallelism, each\\\\nGPU maintains a sharded KV cache. There is no need for additional synchronization because the tree\\\\noperations are the same. Data parallelism with multiple workers is discussed in Sec. A.4 (Appendix).\\\\n4\\\\nEfficient Constrained Decoding with Compressed Finite State Machine\\\\nIn LM programs, users often want to constrain the model’s output to follow specific formats, such\\\\nas JSON schemas. This can improve controllability and robustness, and make the output easier to\\\\nparse. SGLang offers a regex argument to enforce such constraints using regular expressions, which\\\\nare expressive enough for many practical scenarios. Existing systems support this by converting a\\\\nregular expression into a finite state machine (FSM) [54]. During decoding, they maintain the current\\\\nFSM state, retrieve allowed tokens from the next states, and set the probability of invalid tokens to\\\\nzero, decoding token by token. This token-by-token approach, however, is inefficient when there are\\\\nopportunities to decode multiple tokens at once. For example, the constant sequence {\\\\\\\"summary\\\\\\\":\\\\n\\\\\\\" in Fig. 2 spans multiple tokens in the normal decoding process as shown in Fig. 4 (c), requiring\\\\nmultiple decoding stages, even though there is only one valid next token when decoding it. Therefore,\\\\nthe whole sequence can be decoded in a single step (i.e., forward pass). However, existing systems\\\\ncan only decode one token at a time because the lack of integration between the FSM and the model\\\\nrunner in existing systems prevents multi-token processing, resulting in slow decoding.\\\\nSGLang overcomes this limitation by creating a fast constrained decoding runtime with a compressed\\\\nFSM. This runtime analyzes the FSM and compresses adjacent singular-transition edges in the FSM\\\\ninto single edges as demonstrated in Fig. 4 (b), allowing it to recognize when multiple tokens can be\\\\ndecoded together. In Fig. 4 (d), multiple tokens on the compressed transition edge can be decoded in\\\\none forward pass, which greatly accelerates the decoding process. It is also general and applicable to\\\\nall regular expressions. More details on the background and implementation are in Appendix B.\\\\n5\\\\nEfficient Endpoint Calling with API Speculative Execution\\\\nThe previous sections introduced optimizations for open-weight models, which require modifications\\\\nto the model inference process. Additionally, SGLang works with API-access-only models, such as\\\\nOpenAI’s GPT-4. However, for these models, we can only call a black-box API endpoint.\\\\nThis section introduces a new optimization for black-box API models that accelerates execution\\\\nand reduces the API cost of multi-call SGLang programs using speculative execution. For ex-\\\\nample, a program may ask the model to generate a description of a character with a multi-call\\\\n2In practice, the computation is not the same as what is described in the proof of Theorem 3.1 because the\\\\nunpredictable number of output tokens can cause the recomputation of the KV cache.\\\\n6\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 7 ---\\\\nMMLU\\\\nReAct\\\\nAgents\\\\nGenerative\\\\nAgents\\\\nTree of\\\\nThought\\\\nSkeleton\\\\nof Thought\\\\nLLM Judge HellaSwag\\\\nJSON\\\\nDecoding\\\\nMulti-Turn\\\\nChat(short)\\\\nMulti-Turn\\\\n Chat(long)\\\\nDSPy RAG\\\\nPipeline\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.2\\\\n0.5\\\\n0.8\\\\n1.0\\\\nThroughput\\\\n(Normalized)\\\\nSGLang\\\\nvLLM\\\\nGuidance\\\\nLMQL\\\\nFigure 5: Normalized throughput on Llama-7B models. Higher is better.\\\\npattern: s += context + \\\\\\\"name:\\\\\\\" + gen(\\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\", stop=\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\") + \\\\\\\"job:\\\\\\\" + gen(\\\\\\\"job\\\\\\\",\\\\nstop=\\\\\\\"\\\\\\\\n\\\\\\\"). Naively, the two gen primitives correspond to two API calls, meaning that the user\\\\nneeds to pay for the input token fee on the context twice. In SGLang, we can enable speculative\\\\nexecution on the first call and let it continue the generation of a few more tokens by ignoring the stop\\\\ncondition. The interpreter keeps the additional generation outputs and matches and reuses them with\\\\nlater primitives. In certain cases, with careful prompt engineering, the model can correctly match the\\\\ntemplate with high accuracy, saving us the latency and input costs of one API call.\\\\n6\\\\nEvaluation\\\\nWe evaluate the performance of SGLang across diverse LLM workloads. Subsequently, we conduct\\\\nablation studies and case studies to demonstrate the effectiveness of specific components. SGLang is\\\\nimplemented in PyTorch [37] with custom CUDA kernels from FlashInfer [59] and Triton [48].\\\\n6.1\\\\nSetup\\\\nModels. We test dense Llama-2 models [49], sparse mixture of experts Mixtral models [17], multi-\\\\nmodal LLaVA image [27] and video models [62], and API model OpenAI’s GPT-3.5. For open-weight\\\\nmodels, the number of parameters ranges from 7 billion to 70 billion, and we use float16 precision.\\\\nHardware. We run most experiments on AWS EC2 G5 instances, which are equipped with NVIDIA\\\\nA10G GPUs (24GB). We run 7B models on a single A10G GPU and larger models on multiple A10G\\\\nGPUs with tensor parallelism [44]. We run some additional experiments on A100G (80GB) GPUs.\\\\nBaselines. We compare SGLang against both high-level programming systems with their respective\\\\nlanguages and default runtimes, as well as low-level inference engines with standard OpenAI-like\\\\nCompletion APIs. Unless otherwise stated, we do not turn on optimizations that will change the\\\\ncomputation results so that all systems compute the same results. The baselines include:\\\\n• Guidance[13], a language for controlling LLMs. We use Guidance v0.1.8 with llama.cpp backend.\\\\n• vLLM [23], a high-throughput inference engine. We use vLLM v0.2.5 and its default API server3.\\\\n• LMQL [4], a query language. We use LMQL v0.7.3 with Hugging Face Transformers backend.\\\\nWorkloads. We test the following: 5-shot MMLU [14] and 20-shot HellaSwag [61] benchmarks.\\\\nWe decode one token for MMLU and use primitive select to select the answer with the highest\\\\nprobability for HellaSwag. For the ReAct agent [57] and generative agents [36], we extract the\\\\ntraces from the original papers and replay them. We use the Tree-of-thought [56] for the GSM-8K\\\\nproblems and Skeleton-of-thought [33] for tip generation. We use LLM judges with the branch-solve-\\\\nmerge [40] technique; JSON decoding with a schema specified by a regular expression; Multi-turn\\\\nchat with 4 turns, where the input of each turn is randomly sampled between 256-512 tokens. Multi-\\\\nturn chat (short) means short output (4-8 tokens) and multi-turn chat (long) means long output\\\\n(256-512 tokens); DSPy retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) pipeline [20] in its official example.\\\\nMetrics. We report two performance metrics: throughput and latency. For throughput, we run a\\\\nsufficiently large batch of program instances to compute the maximum throughput, comparing the\\\\nnumber of program instances executed per second (programs per second, p/s). For latency, we execute\\\\na single program at a time without batching and report the average latency for multiple instances.\\\\n6.2\\\\nEnd-to-End Performance\\\\nResults on open-weight models. The latency and throughput results are shown in Fig. 5 and Fig. 6.\\\\nSGLang improves throughput by up to 6.4× and reduces latency by up to 3.7×. These improvements\\\\n3RadixAttention has been partially integrated as an optional experimental feature into the latest version of\\\\nvLLM; therefore, we used an earlier version for comparison.\\\\n7\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 8 ---\\\\nMMLU\\\\nReAct\\\\nAgents\\\\nGenerative\\\\nAgents\\\\nTree of\\\\nThought\\\\nSkeleton\\\\nof Thought\\\\nLLM Judge HellaSwag\\\\nJSON\\\\nDecoding\\\\nMulti-Turn\\\\nChat(short)\\\\nMulti-Turn\\\\n Chat(long)\\\\nDSPy RAG\\\\nPipeline\\\\n0.0\\\\n0.2\\\\n0.5\\\\n0.8\\\\n1.0\\\\nLatency\\\\n(Normalized)\\\\nSGLang\\\\nvLLM\\\\nGuidance\\\\nLMQL\\\\nFigure 6: Normalized latency on Llama-7B models. Higher is better.\\\\nresult from KV cache reuse, the exploitation of parallelism within a single program, and faster\\\\nconstrained decoding. Next, we explain the reasons for the speedup in each benchmark.\\\\nOn MMLU, SGLang can reuse the KV cache of the 5-shot examples with RadixAttention. RadixAt-\\\\ntention benefits both throughput and latency. RadixAttention reduces total memory usage by sharing\\\\nthe KV cache, allowing for a larger batch size to improve maximum throughput. RadixAttention\\\\nalso reduces the computation of prefill, thus decreasing the first token latency. On HellaSwag,\\\\nSGLang reuses the KV cache of both few-shot examples and the common question prefix for multiple\\\\nchoices, resulting in two-level sharing. For the ReAct and generative agents, SGLang reuses the\\\\nKV cache of the agent template and previous calls. On Tree-of-thought and Skeleton-of-thought,\\\\nSGLang parallelizes the generation calls within a single program and reuses the KV cache as much\\\\nas possible. On JSON decoding, SGLang accelerates decoding by decoding multiple tokens at once\\\\nwith a compressed finite state machine. In multi-turn chat, SGLang reuses the KV cache of the chat\\\\nhistory. The speedup is more noticeable for short outputs because KV cache reuse mostly helps\\\\nreduce the prefix time. For long outputs, because there is not much sharing between different chat\\\\nsessions and the decoding time dominates, there is almost no speedup. In the DSPy RAG pipeline,\\\\nSGLang reuses the KV cache of the common context example. On these benchmarks, the cache hit\\\\nrate ranges from 50% to 99%. Fig. 13 (Appendix) lists the achieved and optimal cache hit rates for all\\\\nof them, showing that our cache-aware scheduling approaches 96% of the optimal hit rate on average.\\\\nWe exclude LMQL and Guidance from some of the last five benchmarks due to slow performance and\\\\nmissing functionalities. LMQL’s issues stem from slow token-level processing and an unoptimized\\\\nbackend, while Guidance lacks batching and parallelism support.\\\\nResults on larger models with tensor parallelism. We run larger models, Mixtral-8x7B and Llama-\\\\n70B, with tensor parallelism on the same set of benchmarks and report the results in Fig. 7 and Fig. 12\\\\n(Appendix). The speedup on larger models shows a trend similar to that observed on smaller models,\\\\nindicating that our optimization generalizes well to larger models. We omit Guidance and LMQL\\\\nhere because they lack efficient implementations of tensor parallelism.\\\\nResults on multi-modal models. SGLang has native support for multi-modal models with the\\\\nimage and video primitives. The optimizations in this paper are compatible with multi-modal\\\\nmodels. For RadixAttention, we compute the hash of the input images and use it as the key in the\\\\nradix tree, allowing us to reuse the KV cache of the image tokens from the same image. We run\\\\nLLaVA-v1.5-7B (image) on llava-bench-in-the-wild and LLaVA-NeXT-34B (video) on ActivityNet.\\\\nBecause these models are not well supported by other baseline systems, we use the model authors’\\\\noriginal implementation in Hugging Face Transformers as the baseline. As shown in Table 2, SGLang\\\\nprovides throughput up to 6× higher on these benchmarks. In llava-bench-in-the-wild, there are\\\\nmultiple questions about the same image, and SGLang runtime reuses the KV cache in this case.\\\\nProduction deployment. SGLang has been deployed in Chatbot Arena [8] to serve open-weight\\\\nmodels. Due to low traffic for some models, only one SGLang worker serves each. After one\\\\nmonth, we observed a 52.4% RadixAttention cache hit rate for LLaVA-Next-34B [28] and 74.1% for\\\\nVicuna-33B [7]. Cache hits come from common system messages, frequently reused example images,\\\\nand multi-turn chat histories. This reduces first-token latency by an average of 1.7× for Vicuna-33B.\\\\n8\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 9 ---\\\\nTable 2: Throughput comparison on multi-modal LLaVA image and video models.\\\\nModel\\\\nLLaVA-v1.5-7B (image)\\\\nLLaVA-NeXT-34B (video)\\\\nAuthor’s original implementation\\\\n0.18 image/s\\\\n0.02 frame/s\\\\nSGLang\\\\n1.15 image/s\\\\n0.10 frame/s\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80 100\\\\nCache Hit Rate (%)\\\\n20\\\\n30\\\\n40\\\\n(a)\\\\nBatch Size\\\\nThroughput (tokens / s)\\\\n0\\\\n20\\\\n40\\\\n60\\\\n80 100\\\\nCache Hit Rate (%)\\\\n200\\\\n300\\\\n400\\\\n(b)\\\\nTotal Latency (s)\\\\nFirst Token Latency (s)\\\\nLLM Judge\\\\nTree of\\\\nThought\\\\nMMLU\\\\nMulti-Turn\\\\nChat(short)\\\\n0.00\\\\n0.25\\\\n0.50\\\\n0.75\\\\n1.00\\\\nThroughput\\\\n(Normalized)\\\\n(c)\\\\nNo Cache\\\\nNo Tree Structure\\\\nFCFS Schedule\\\\nRandom Schedule\\\\nNo Frontend Parallelism\\\\nNo Frontend Hint\\\\nFull Optimization\\\\n0.4k\\\\n0.6k\\\\n0.8k\\\\n1.0k\\\\n1.2k\\\\n10\\\\n20\\\\nFigure 8: (a)(b) Cache hit rate ablation study. By using few-shot prompting, the accuracy of API speculative execution\\\\nis high, and it reduces the cost of input tokens by about threefold due to the extraction of three fields.\\\\n6.3\\\\nAblation Study\\\\nCache hit rate vs. latency/throughput. Fig. 8(a)(b) shows the relationship between cache hit\\\\nrate and performance metrics (first token latency, total latency, batch size, and throughput) on the\\\\ntree-of-thought benchmark. The figure is obtained by partially disabling matched tokens at runtime.\\\\nIt shows that a higher cache hit rate leads to a larger batch size, higher throughput, and lower latency.\\\\nEffectiveness of RadixAttention. We test the effectiveness of RadixAttention and its components\\\\non several representative benchmarks. As shown in Fig. 8(c), \\\\\\\"No Cache\\\\\\\" means not using any\\\\ncache, \\\\\\\"No Tree-Structure\\\\\\\" means using a simple table-based cache instead of a tree-structured cache,\\\\n\\\\\\\"FCFS Schedule\\\\\\\" means using a first-come-first-serve policy instead of our cache-aware scheduling,\\\\n\\\\\\\"Random Schedule\\\\\\\" means using a random order to schedule requests, \\\\\\\"No Frontend Parallelism\\\\\\\"\\\\nmeans disabling parallelism in the interpreter, \\\\\\\"No Frontend Hint\\\\\\\" means disabling sending the\\\\nfork hints from the interpreters, and \\\\\\\"Full optimizations\\\\\\\" means we turn on all optimizations. The\\\\nexperimental results show that each of these components is required to achieve the best performance.\\\\nDisabling parallelism and hints from the frontend interpreter also results in suboptimal runtime\\\\nperformance, highlighting the importance of co-designing the frontend language and runtime.\\\\nOverhead of RadixAttention. We test the overhead of RadixAttention on a benchmark without any\\\\nKV cache reuse opportunities. The benchmark measures throughput on the ShareGPT dataset. It\\\\ntakes 74.3 seconds to run 100 requests; however, the time used for managing the RadixAttention data\\\\nstructures is only 0.2 seconds, which is a negligible overhead of less than 0.3%. This is because the\\\\ncomplexity of tree operations is linear and small. Thus, we can turn on RadixAttention by default.\\\\nEffectiveness of the compressed finite state machine. We test the effectiveness of the compressed\\\\nfinite state machine and its components on the JSON decoding benchmark. Experimental results\\\\nshow that the compressed finite state machine increases the throughput by 1.6× because it can decode\\\\nmultiple tokens at once. In addition, we need to preprocess the state machine and reuse it for a batch\\\\nof requests. Otherwise, redoing the preprocessing for each request makes the throughput 2.4× lower.\\\\n7\\\\nRelated Work\\\\nVarious works have explored the reuse of the KV cache, and many of them are concurrent with our\\\\nwork. Uniquely, our RadixAttention first proposes treating the KV cache as a tree-based LRU cache.\\\\nIt is the first solution that supports multi-level sharing, cache-aware scheduling, frontend-runtime\\\\nco-scheduling, and distributed cases. vLLM [23] and ChunkedAttention [58] explore some simple\\\\nreuse cases (e.g., system prompt sharing) but do not cover multi-level tree-structured sharing or LRU\\\\ncaching. PromptCache [12] proposes the modular reuse of the KV cache beyond the prefix but can\\\\nimpact accuracy by up to a 43% drop. HydraGen [18], FlashInfer [59], and ChunkedAttention [58]\\\\nfocus on CUDA kernel optimizations and do not include the concept of an LRU cache. API Serve [1]\\\\nand LLM-SQL [29] study KV cache reuse for specific applications such as interleaving with external\\\\nAPI calls and relational databases, but they do not have our radix tree or cache-aware scheduling.\\\\n9\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 10 ---\\\\nSeveral LLM programming and agent frameworks exist, such as Guidance [13], LMQL [4],\\\\nDSPy [20], LangChain [24], AutoGen [55], and LLM Compiler [21]. Guidance and LMQL are most\\\\nsimilar to SGLang, and we compare them in Sec. 2. Our innovation lies in novel runtime optimizations\\\\nfor accelerating the proposed programming model. SGLang is compatible with other frameworks and\\\\ncan accelerate them (e.g., the DSPy example in our evaluation). Additionally, SGLang is compatible\\\\nwith many other common inference optimizations [60, 39, 3, 23, 59, 10, 26, 15, 19, 32, 31, 11].\\\\n8\\\\nFuture Directions and Conclusion\\\\nFuture directions. Despite the progress made with SGLang, several limitations remain that reveal\\\\npromising directions for future research. These include extending SGLang to support additional\\\\noutput modalities, adapting RadixAttention to operate across multiple levels of the memory hierarchy\\\\n(e.g., DRAM, Disk) [43], enabling fuzzy semantic matching within RadixAttention, providing higher-\\\\nlevel primitives atop SGLang, fixing starvation in cache-aware scheduling [42], and enhancing the\\\\nSGLang compiler to perform advanced static optimizations such as scheduling and memory planning.\\\\nConclusion. We introduce SGLang, a framework for efficient programming and executing structured\\\\nlanguage model programs. SGLang significantly improves the throughput and latency of complex\\\\nLM programs through novel optimizations like RadixAttention, compressed finite state machines,\\\\nand a language interpreter. It is a valuable tool for developing advanced prompting techniques and\\\\nagent workflows. The source code is publicly available.\\\\nAcknowledgement\\\\nThis project is supported by the Stanford Center for Automated Reasoning and gifts from Astronomer,\\\\nGoogle, IBM, Intel, Lacework, Microsoft, Mohamed Bin Zayed University of Artificial Intelligence,\\\\nNexla, Samsung SDS, Uber, and VMware. Shareable elements\\\\ninclude few-shot learning examples, questions in self-consistency [53], chat history in multi-turn\\\\nchat, and search history in tree-of-thought [56].\\\\nA\\\\nAdditional Details on RadixAttention\\\\nA.1\\\\nBackground on the KV Cache\\\\nMost LLMs in use today, such as GPT-3 [5], PaLM [9], and LLaMA [49], are based on the autore-\\\\ngressive Transformer architecture [51]. These models predict the probability of the next token in a\\\\nsequence based on the preceding tokens. During inference, the model first processes a sequence of\\\\ninput tokens through a forward pass (this process is called \\\\\\\"prefill\\\\\\\"). It then sequentially decodes\\\\noutput tokens, with each token depending on prior tokens (this process is called \\\\\\\"decoding\\\\\\\"). We\\\\nrefer to the process of taking a sequence of input tokens and generating a sequence of output tokens\\\\nas a single-generation call. Throughout this process, each token generates some intermediate tensors,\\\\nwhich are used for decoding further tokens. These intermediate tensors, known as the \\\\\\\"KV Cache,\\\\\\\"\\\\nare named for the key-value pairs in the self-attention mechanism. An important observation when\\\\ndiscussing optimizations in this paper is that the computation of the KV cache only depends on all\\\\nprevious tokens, so different sequences with the same prefix can reuse the KV cache of the prefix\\\\ntokens and avoid redundant computation.\\\\nOften in LLM programs, multiple text segments and generation calls are appended to a single\\\\nprompt. Caching the computed KV cache for previous tokens across multiple chained calls can\\\\nreduce redundant computation. This optimization, however, is neither free nor trivial, as it requires\\\\nadditional storage and more complex memory management. In addition, it is common in LLM\\\\nprograms to generate multiple outputs from a single prompt or to fork a new prompt from the current\\\\nstate [25]. Basic prefix sharing has been investigated in vLLM [23]. More advanced sharing patterns\\\\nlike irregular tree-structured sharing can also be employed. Fig. 9 shows four typical patterns of KV\\\\ncache sharing across multiple calls; none of the existing systems can automatically handle all of them.\\\\nOn the contrary, our RadixAttention in Sec. 3 can handle all of them automatically at runtime.\\\\nA.2\\\\nPseudocode for Cache-Aware Scheduling\\\\nAlg. 1 shows the pseudocode of cache-aware scheduling for RadixAttention with continuous batching.\\\\nA.3\\\\nProof of the Theorem 3.1\\\\nTheorem 3.1. For a batch of requests, we can achieve an optimal cache hit rate by visiting the radix\\\\ntree of the requests in the depth-first search order, with a cache size ≥the maximum request length.\\\\nThe longest-shared-prefix-first order is equivalent to a depth-first search order.\\\\nProof. First, we show that the depth-first search (DFS) order achieves an optimal cache hit rate. Let\\\\nR denote the set of requests in the batch, and T denote the radix tree built from R. For each edge e\\\\nof T, the KV cache associated with e needs to be computed at least once. Let |e| denote the size of\\\\nthe KV cache associated with e. Let C denote the computational complexity of the KV cache for R.\\\\n14\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 15 ---\\\\nAlgorithm 1 Cache-Aware Scheduling for RadixAttention with Continuous Batching.\\\\nInput: The radix tree T, the memory pool P, the current running batch B, the waiting queue Q.\\\\nOutput: Finished requests and updated system state.\\\\n// Get all requests from the waiting queue\\\\nrequests ←Q.get_all_requests()\\\\n// Search for the prefix matching for all waiting requests\\\\nfor req ∈requests do\\\\nreq.prefix_node, req.prefix_len ←T.match_prefix(req.input_tokens)\\\\nend for\\\\n// Sort the requests according to the matched prefix lenghts\\\\nrequests.sort()\\\\n// Select requests for the next batch\\\\navailable_size ←T.evictable_size() + P.available_size()\\\\ncurrent_size ←0\\\\nnew_batch ←[]\\\\nfor req ∈requests do\\\\nif req.size() + current_size < available_size then\\\\nnew_batch.append(req)\\\\ndelta ←T.increase_ref_counter(req.prefix_node)\\\\navailable_size ←available_size + delta\\\\nend if\\\\nend for\\\\nQ.remove_requests(new_batch)\\\\n// Insert requests into the current running batch\\\\nB.merge(new_batch)\\\\n// Allocate new memory and do eviction if necessary\\\\nneeded_size ←B.needed_size()\\\\nsuccess, buffer ←P.alloc(needed_size)\\\\nif not success then\\\\nT.evict(needed_size)\\\\nsuccess, buffer ←P.alloc(needed_size)\\\\nend if\\\\nB.run(buffer)\\\\n// Process finished requests\\\\nfinished_requests ←B.drop_finished_requests()\\\\nfor req ∈finished_requests do\\\\nT.decrease_ref_counter(req.prefix_node)\\\\nT.insert(req)\\\\nend for\\\\nreturn finished_requests\\\\nWe obtain the lower bound\\\\nC ≥\\\\nX\\\\ne∈edges(T )\\\\n|e|.\\\\nConsider we visit the radix tree T in DFS order. For each edge e of T, the first time we compute the\\\\nKV cache associated with e, we will then compute the whole subtree of e. During the computation of\\\\nthe subtree of e, the edge e will be continuously hit, so no additional computation will happen. After\\\\nfinishing the computation for the subtree rooted at e, the edge e will not be visited again. Notice that,\\\\nwith a cache size ≥the maximum request length, which equals the longest path in the radix tree T,\\\\nedge e will not be evicted during the computation of its subtree, since the common prefix including e\\\\nof the subtree will be continuously hit. Therefore, the KV cache associated with each edge e will be\\\\ncomputed only once. Thus, we achieve the lower bound\\\\nC =\\\\nX\\\\ne∈edges(T )\\\\n|e|.\\\\n15\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 16 ---\\\\nThe cache hit rate, defined asP\\\\nr∈R number of cached prefill tokens in r\\\\nP\\\\nr∈R number of prefill tokens in r\\\\n,\\\\nequals 1 −\\\\nC\\\\nP\\\\nr∈R number of prefill tokens, reaches its upper bound, delivering optimality.\\\\nNext, we show that the longest-shared-prefix-first order is equivalent to a DFS order by induction.\\\\n• (Base) In the beginning, since there is nothing cached, a random request that corresponds to\\\\na node x in T will be processed. All requests that correspond to the nodes {v1, ..., vn} on the\\\\npath from the root to x do not need a recomputation. The computation complexity for requests\\\\ncorresponding to the nodes {v1, ..., vn, x} is aligned with a valid DFS. The path from the root to\\\\nx is cached.\\\\n• (Induction) Assume we just visited a node y in T, and the visited nodes align with a DFS order.\\\\nLet P denote the path from the root to y. Then each node that has not been visited has the lowest\\\\ncommon ancestor with the visited nodes on P. Since nodes on P are cached, a node z that has\\\\nnot been visited with the lowest common ancestor on P will have the longest shared prefix. The\\\\nlongest-shared-prefix-first order will select z, which is a valid DFS order. The path from the root\\\\nto z will be cached because it is the most recent.\\\\nIn the online case, the DFS order will be disrupted, but the longest shared prefix schedule still\\\\napproximates the DFS behavior on the augmented part of the implied radix tree. We show this by\\\\nconsidering the step of adding a new batch of requests.\\\\nLet T denote the part of the radix tree that has been visited so far, and T ′ denote the whole new\\\\nradix tree after adding the new batch of requests. Let C denote the set of cached nodes in T. Let\\\\nlongest(C) denote the node in C that has the longest path from the root and has a subtree in T ′ that\\\\nhas not been fully visited.\\\\nThe longest shared prefix schedule will then process the subtree in T ′ rooted at longest(C) in a DFS\\\\norder. During this process, eviction could occur, and the remaining cached nodes from C become\\\\nC(1) ⊆C. A DFS will then occur for the subtree in T ′ rooted at longest(C(1)).\\\\nSimilarly, we will have C(2), . . . , C(k), until C(k) contains only one leaf node in C(k) that has its\\\\nsubtree in T ′ not fully visited. At this point, we have reached a valid DFS state. The remaining part\\\\nof T ′ will be visited in DFS order as described in the proof of Theorem 3.1.\\\\nA.4\\\\nData-Parallel Distributed RadixAttention\\\\nTo adapt the RadixAttention for distributed settings with multiple replica workers (i.e., data par-\\\\nallelism), we developed a mechanism wherein each worker maintains its own sub-tree, while the\\\\nrouter oversees a meta-tree. This meta-tree acts as a trie that tracks all sub-trees and their associated\\\\ndevices. Upon the arrival of a new batch of requests at the router, prefix matching is executed on the\\\\nmeta-tree. We implement various policies based on each request’s affinity—measured by the length\\\\nof the shared prefix with specific workers and other requests in the same group—to make efficient\\\\ndispatch decisions that minimize redundant computations. Each time new requests are processed,\\\\nboth the router and workers independently update their respective trees. Should an eviction occur\\\\nat a worker node, it commits this eviction to a queue, which the router then processes to update the\\\\nmeta-tree during periods of low activity. We benchmarked this distributed configuration using four\\\\nworkers and the MMLU dataset, observing that it achieves linear scaling and an optimal cache hit rate\\\\nwith minimal overhead from this weakly consistent distributed cache design. There exists a trade-off\\\\nbetween maximizing data locality and parallel processing efficiency. Exploring advanced scheduling\\\\npolicies to optimize this trade-off is designated as an area for future research. In addition, concurrent\\\\nwork from Preble [45] studies data-parallel scheduling based on an early version of SGLang.\\\\nB\\\\nAdditional Details on Compressed Finite State Machine\\\\nThis section discusses the background and implementation details of the compressed finite state\\\\nmachine for faster constrained decoding. We aim for LLMs to follow a regular expression (regex),\\\\n16\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 17 ---\\\\nwhich offers greater expressiveness and can be used to represent common formats such as JSON\\\\nschemas. To achieve this, we convert the regex into a Finite State Machine (FSM) to guide the\\\\ngeneration process during decoding [54]. An FSM is essentially a graph with nodes (states) and\\\\nedges (transitions with strings/characters). Starting from an initial state, each transition appends the\\\\nstring on the edge to move to the next state, using a set of final states to conclude the process. This\\\\nmechanism guides an LLM’s decoding, filtering out invalid tokens based on the FSM’s current state\\\\ntransitions, as illustrated in Fig. 10. The decoding might involve multiple transitions in the FSM\\\\nuntil reaching a final state.\\\\n§ age\\\\n§ Age\\\\n§ hou\\\\n§ 0\\\\n§ 1\\\\n§ ﬁf\\\\n…\\\\nDecode + FSM\\\\nConstrained Decoding With Logits Mask \\\\nDecoding Status\\\\nRegular Expression\\\\n0\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n1\\\\na\\\\n2\\\\ng\\\\n3\\\\ne\\\\n4\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\n6\\\\n[0-9]\\\\n5\\\\n:\\\\n[0-9]\\\\n7\\\\n,\\\\nFinite State Machine\\\\nDecoding Status\\\\nDecode + FSM\\\\n✔\\\\n✖\\\\nallowed next token\\\\nnot allowed next token \\\\n✔\\\\n✔\\\\n✖\\\\n✔\\\\n✖\\\\n✖\\\\nFigure 10: Example of how regex is converted into FSM and how FSM guides the decoding process.\\\\nThe challenge of constrained decoding arises from the fact that constraints are often expressed in\\\\nnatural language formats, i.e., regex is depicted by characters/strings, while LLMs are designed to\\\\ninterpret and process these as tokens. This creates a complex scenario since the mapping between\\\\nstrings and tokens is intricate and lacks a one-to-one correspondence [22].\\\\nThis section is derived from an earlier blog post4. Readers are also encouraged to read the blog post\\\\nfor additional background and easier understanding.\\\\nB.1\\\\nImplementation Details of Compressed Finite State Machine\\\\nTo simplify the construction of Compressed FSM, we build the original FSM on characters/strings\\\\ninstead of on tokens. We formally define the concepts of singular transition edge and compressed\\\\nedge as follows:\\\\n• Singular transition edge: A edge is a singular transition edge if 1) its source node has only one\\\\nsuccessor node, and 2) there is only one acceptable character/string on it.\\\\n• Compressed edge: An edge compressed by several consecutively adjacent edges (e0, e1, . . . , ek)\\\\nif and only if e1, . . . , ek are singular transition edges. The text of the compressed edge is the\\\\nconcatenation of the texts of e0, e1, . . . , ek.\\\\nStarting from an FSM based on characters, we recursively merge singular transition edges into\\\\ntheir preceding ones until further compression is unfeasible, resulting in a Compressed FSM. This\\\\napproach speeds up the decoding process, as demonstrated by SGLang’s runtime efficiency with the\\\\nCompressed FSM, shown in Fig. 11.\\\\nB.2\\\\nHandling Tokenization Artifacts with Retokenization\\\\nWhen a new token is generated, we get the token’s string and search all the outgoing edges of the\\\\ncurrent state find the one that starts with the just decoded string, and then move forward. However,\\\\nwhen the transition edge is a well-compressed one and contains a very long string, we may anticipate\\\\nthe next rounds’ decoded strings as well. This is where the acceleration happens and we call this\\\\nprocess Jump Forward. However, we still need to convert the string into tokens for the next decoding\\\\nphases and it is not straightforward due to the LLM’s specific pretraining and tokenization method;\\\\n4https://lmsys.org/blog/2024-02-05-compressed-fsm/\\\\n17\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 18 ---\\\\nPlease fill in the following \\\\n    information about Harry Potter.\\\\n{\\\\n▁▁▁▁\\\\\\\"name\\\\\\\": ▁\\\\\\\"\\\\nHar\\\\n▁Pot\\\\n\\\\\\\",\\\\nter\\\\n1\\\\nry\\\\n▁▁▁▁ \\\\\\\"age\\\\\\\" :▁\\\\n1\\\\n,\\\\n▁▁▁▁\\\\\\\"house\\\\\\\":▁\\\\\\\"\\\\nG\\\\nryffindor\\\\\\\",\\\\n}\\\\n</s>\\\\nPlease fill in the following \\\\ninformation about Harry Potter.\\\\n{\\\\n\\\\\\\\n\\\\n▁\\\\n▁▁\\\\n▁\\\\\\\"\\\\nname\\\\n\\\\\\\":\\\\nHar\\\\nry\\\\n▁Pot\\\\nter\\\\n\\\\\\\",\\\\n\\\\\\\\n\\\\n▁▁\\\\n▁\\\\n▁\\\\\\\"\\\\nage\\\\n▁\\\\\\\"\\\\n\\\\\\\":\\\\n▁\\\\n1\\\\n1\\\\n,\\\\n\\\\\\\\n\\\\n▁▁\\\\n▁▁\\\\n\\\\\\\"\\\\nh\\\\nous\\\\ne\\\\n\\\\\\\":\\\\n▁\\\\\\\"\\\\nG\\\\nry\\\\nff\\\\nind\\\\nor\\\\n\\\\\\\",\\\\n\\\\\\\\n\\\\n}\\\\n</s>\\\\nJump-Forward Decode With Compressed FSM\\\\nNormal Decode With FSM\\\\nPreﬁll\\\\nDecode\\\\nJump-Forward\\\\nGenerated JSONs\\\\nFigure 11: Comparison of decoding using Compressed FSM versus normal FSM: The left subfigure\\\\ndepicts the decoding process per forward pass, while the right subfigure explains the origins of various\\\\nresult components.\\\\ndirect partitioning might alter the intended meaning [50]. For example, the compressed text in Fig. 2’s\\\\nregex is {\\\\\\\"summary\\\\\\\": \\\\\\\", which can only be tokenized as {\\\\\\\", summary, \\\\\\\": and _\\\\\\\" according to\\\\nthe tokenizer instead of partition them randomly such as {\\\\\\\", summa, ry, and \\\\\\\":_\\\\\\\". To address this\\\\nissue, we use the original tokenizer to retokenize all the previous text as well as the text of the\\\\ncompressed edge, ensuring alignment with the original input format of LLMs. And it only brings\\\\nminor retokenization overhead.\\\\nB.3\\\\nFuture Extension: Addressing Distorted Probability\\\\nThe challenge caused by the gap between strings and tokens also brings the problem of skewed proba-\\\\nbility distribution [50]. For example, in Fig. 2, the regex \\\\\\\"[ABCD][+-]?\\\\\\\" suggests grades from A+ to\\\\nD-, but if replaced with broader terms like Excellent|Above Average|Fair|Below Average,\\\\nthe runtime may inaccurately map an A to Above Average due to the term Above Average is on a\\\\ncompressed transition, misrepresenting the grade hierarchy. This occurs because the LLM doesn’t\\\\nrecognize the specific range of choices, leading to inappropriate token sequences. Computing accurate\\\\nprobabilities for each choice requires summing the probabilities of all token sequences that result\\\\nin each choice, which complicates decoding and adds overhead. One workaround is to include the\\\\nchoices or the regex directly in the prefill prompt, guiding the LLM to be aware of its choices and\\\\noutput the decision in proper token sequences. However, this approach doesn’t solve the underlying\\\\nissue of distorted probabilities, highlighting the need for further research to improve the compressed\\\\nFSM’s accuracy.\\\\nC\\\\nAdditional Experimental Setups and Results\\\\nAdditional experimental setups. Fig. 8(c) is obtained by running Llama-7B on a single A10G (24GB) GPU. Fig. 12\\\\nare obtained by running Llama-70B on 4 A100G (80GB) GPUs with tensor parallelism. This graph includes nodes for primitive operators\\\\nand edges for dependencies. See Fig. 14b for the graph corresponding to the program in Fig. 14a. In\\\\nthe program, each call to a decorated function or fork creates a new prompt state or a stream.\\\\nThere are several types of nodes. Each operand of the operators += and + in a SGLang program\\\\nis represented by an IR node. These include ConstantText, Argument, Gen, Select, Variable,\\\\nFork, GetForkItem, and Join. There are two types of dependencies: intra-stream dependency,\\\\nwhere operations submitted into a stream using += must be executed after all preceding operations\\\\nin that stream, and inter-stream dependency, which occurs when one stream needs to fetch variable\\\\nvalues from another stream, necessitating synchronization. Operations like fork manipulate multiple\\\\nstreams and thus introduce inter-stream dependencies.\\\\nTo generate the graph, we use tracing to run the program with abstract arguments and construct\\\\nthe graph dynamically. This method is limited to programs without data-dependent control flow, a\\\\nlimitation we plan to address in future work. Once constructed, the graph can be executed through\\\\na graph executor, eliminating the need to reinterpret the original Python program. This results in\\\\nbenefits like graph rewriting optimizations, reduced runtime overhead, and program serialization. For\\\\nexecution, stream executors are launched for each data stream, dispatching IR nodes to the streams in\\\\ntopological order.\\\\nD.2\\\\nA Case Study of Compiler Optimization: Code Movement for Improving Prefix Sharing\\\\nWe explore a compilation optimization for SGLang IR: code movement for improving prefix sharing.\\\\nWe anticipate that more classical compiler techniques can also be applied, such as auto-tuning and\\\\ninstruction selection.\\\\nThis optimization aims to improve prefix sharing by reordering nodes in the graph to increase the\\\\nlength of the constant prefix. This\\\\noptimization is interesting because traditional program analysis cannot achieve it due to the presence\\\\nof natural language instructions in SGLang. We\\\\nwrite a prompt with several examples to teach GPT-4 the concepts of SGLang IR, and we find that\\\\nGPT-4 can successfully apply this optimization for some simple SGLang Since these models generate a next token in an au-\\\\ntoregressive manner, one has to run the model multiple times\\\\nto process an inference request where each iteration of the\\\\nmodel generates a single output token for the request. How-\\\\never, existing systems for inference serving do not perform\\\\nwell on this type of workload that has a multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic, due to their inﬂexible scheduling mechanism that\\\\ncannot change the current batch of requests being processed;\\\\nrequests that have ﬁnished earlier than other requests in a\\\\nbatch cannot return to the client, while newly arrived requests\\\\nhave to wait until the current batch completely ﬁnishes.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose iteration-level scheduling, a new\\\\nscheduling mechanism that schedules execution at the gran-\\\\nularity of iteration (instead of request) where the scheduler\\\\ninvokes the execution engine to run only a single iteration of\\\\nthe model on the batch. In addition, to apply batching and\\\\niteration-level scheduling to a Transformer model at the same\\\\ntime, we suggest selective batching, which applies batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations. Based on these two tech-\\\\nniques, we have implemented a distributed serving system\\\\ncalled ORCA, with additional designs for scalability to models\\\\nwith hundreds of billions of parameters. Our evaluation on a\\\\nGPT-3 175B model shows that ORCA can signiﬁcantly out-\\\\nperform NVIDIA FasterTransformer in terms of both latency\\\\nand throughput: 36.9× throughput improvement at the same\\\\nlevel of latency.\\\\n1\\\\nIntroduction\\\\nLanguage generation tasks are becoming increasingly\\\\nparamount to many types of applications, such as chatbot [9,\\\\n52], summarization [41,45,54], code generation [13], and cap-\\\\ntion generation [65,66]. Moreover, recent works published by\\\\n∗Corresponding author.\\\\nAI21 Labs [37], DeepMind [26,48], Google [15,21,63], Meta\\\\nPlatforms [10,67], Microsoft [50], Microsoft & NVIDIA [59],\\\\nand OpenAI [12] have reported that every language process-\\\\ning task, including translation [11,17], classiﬁcation [20,53],\\\\nquestion-answering [32, 33, 40] and more, can be cast as a\\\\nlanguage generation problem and have shown great improve-\\\\nments along this direction. The rise of generative models is\\\\nnot limited to the language domain; the AI community has\\\\nalso given growing interest to generation problems in other do-\\\\nmains such as image, video, speech, or a mixture of multiple\\\\ndomains [19,38,51,62]. At the heart of generative models lies\\\\nthe Transformer architecture [60] and its variants [15,47–49].\\\\nBy relying on the attention mechanism [60], Transformer\\\\nmodels can learn better representations where each element\\\\nof the sequence may have a direct connection with every other\\\\nelement, which was not possible in recurrent models [25].\\\\nTo use generative models in real-world applications, we\\\\noften delegate the inference procedure to a separate service\\\\nresponsible for ML inference serving. The growing demands\\\\nfor this service, which should provide inference results for\\\\nclient requests at low latency and high throughput, have fa-\\\\ncilitated the development of inference serving systems such\\\\nas Triton Inference Server [7] and TensorFlow Serving [42].\\\\nThese systems can use a separately-developed DNN execution\\\\nengine to perform the actual tensor operations. For example,\\\\nwe can deploy a service for language generation tasks by\\\\nusing a combination of Triton and FasterTransformer [4], an\\\\nexecution engine optimized for the inference of Transformer-\\\\nbased models. In this case, Triton is mainly responsible for\\\\ngrouping multiple client requests into a batch, while Faster-\\\\nTransformer receives the batch from Triton and conducts the\\\\ninference procedure in the batched manner.\\\\nUnfortunately, we notice that the existing inference sys-\\\\ntems, including both the serving system layer and the execu-\\\\ntion engine layer, have limitations in handling requests for\\\\nTransformer-based generative models. Since these models are\\\\ntrained to generate a next token in an autoregressive manner,\\\\none should run the model as many times as the number of to-\\\\nkens to generate, while for other models like ResNet [24] and\\\\nUSENIX Association\\\\n16th USENIX Symposium on Operating Systems Design and Implementation    521\\\\n\\\\n\\\\n--- PAGE 3 ---\\\\nBERT [18] a request can be processed by running the model\\\\nonce. That is, in order to process a request to the generative\\\\nmodel, we have to run multiple iterations of the model; each\\\\niteration generates a single output token, which is used as\\\\nan input in the following iteration. Such multi-iteration char-\\\\nacteristic calls into question the current design of inference\\\\nsystems, where the serving system schedules the execution\\\\nof the engine at the granularity of request. Under this design,\\\\nwhen the serving system dispatches a batch of requests to\\\\nthe engine, the engine returns inference results for the entire\\\\nbatch at once after processing all requests within the batch.\\\\nAs different client requests may require different numbers of\\\\niterations for processing, requests that have ﬁnished earlier\\\\nthan others in the batch cannot return to the client, resulting\\\\nin an increased latency. Requests arrived after dispatching the\\\\nbatch also should wait for processing the batch, which can\\\\nsigniﬁcantly increase the requests’ queueing time.\\\\nIn this paper, we propose to schedule the execution of the\\\\nengine at the granularity of iteration instead of request. In\\\\nparticular, the serving system invokes the engine to run only a\\\\nsingle iteration of the model on the batch. As a result, a newly\\\\narrived request can be considered for processing after waiting\\\\nfor only a single iteration of the model. The serving system\\\\nchecks whether a request has ﬁnished processing after every\\\\nreturn from the engine – hence the ﬁnished requests can also\\\\nbe returned to the clients immediately.\\\\nNevertheless, a noticeable challenge arises when we at-\\\\ntempt to apply batching and the iteration-level scheduling at\\\\nthe same time. Unlike the canonical request-level scheduling,\\\\nthe proposed scheduling can issue a batch of requests where\\\\neach request has so far processed a different number of tokens.\\\\nIn such a case, the requests to the Transformer model cannot\\\\nbe processed in the batched manner because the attention\\\\nmechanism calls for non-batchable tensor operations whose\\\\ninput tensors have variable shapes depending on the number\\\\nof processed tokens.\\\\nTo address this challenge, we suggest to apply batching\\\\nonly to a selected set of operations, which we call selective\\\\nbatching. By taking different characteristics of operations into\\\\naccount, selective batching splits the batch and processes each\\\\nrequest individually for the Attention1 operation while apply-\\\\ning batching to other operations of the Transformer model.\\\\nWe observe that the decision not to batch the executions of\\\\nthe Attention operation has only a small impact on efﬁciency.\\\\nSince the Attention operation is not associated with any model\\\\nparameters, applying batching to Attention has no beneﬁt of\\\\nreducing the amount of GPU memory reads by reusing the\\\\nloaded parameters across multiple requests.\\\\nBased on these techniques, we design and implement\\\\nORCA, a distributed serving system for Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models. In order to handle large-scale models,\\\\n1In some literature the Attention operation has an extended deﬁnition that\\\\nincludes linear layers (QKV Linear and Attn Out Linear; Figure 1b). On the\\\\nother hand, we use a narrow deﬁnition as described in Figure 1b.\\\\nORCA adopts parallelization strategies including intra-layer\\\\nand inter-layer model parallelism, which were originally de-\\\\nveloped by training systems [55,58] for Transformer models.\\\\nWe also devise a new scheduling algorithm for the proposed\\\\niteration-level scheduling, with additional considerations for\\\\nmemory management and pipelined execution across work-\\\\ners.\\\\nWe evaluate ORCA using OpenAI GPT-3 [12] models with\\\\nvarious conﬁgurations, scaling up to 341B of parameters. The\\\\nresults show that ORCA signiﬁcantly outperforms FasterTrans-\\\\nformer [4], showing 36.9× throughput improvement at the\\\\nsame level of latency. While we use a language model as\\\\na driving example throughout the paper and conduct experi-\\\\nments only on language models, generative models in other\\\\ndomains can beneﬁt from our approach as long as the mod-\\\\nels are based on the Transformer architecture and use the\\\\nautoregressive generation procedure [19,38,51,62].\\\\n2\\\\nBackground\\\\nWe provide background on the inference procedure of\\\\nGPT [12,47], a representative example of Transformer-based\\\\ngenerative models that we use throughout this paper, and ML\\\\ninference serving systems.\\\\nInference procedure of GPT.\\\\nGPT is an autoregressive\\\\nlanguage model based on one of architectural variants of\\\\nTransformer [60]. It takes text as input and produces new text\\\\nas output. In particular, the model receives a sequence of input\\\\ntokens and then completes the sequence by generating subse-\\\\nquent output tokens. Figure 1a illustrates a simpliﬁed compu-\\\\ntation graph that represents this procedure with a three-layer\\\\nGPT model, where nodes and edges indicate Transformer\\\\nlayers and dependencies between the layers, respectively. The\\\\nTransformer layers are executed in the order denoted by the\\\\nnumbers on the nodes, and the nodes that use the same set\\\\nof model parameters (i.e., nodes representing the same layer)\\\\nare ﬁlled with the same color.\\\\nThe generated output token is fed back into the model to\\\\ngenerate the next output token, imposing a sequential, one-\\\\nby-one inference procedure. This autoregressive procedure of\\\\ngenerating a single token is done by running all the layers of\\\\nthe model with the input, which is either a sequence of input\\\\ntokens that came from the client or a previously generated out-\\\\nput token. We deﬁne the run of all layers as an iteration of the\\\\nmodel. In the example shown in Figure 1a, the inference pro-\\\\ncedure comprises three iterations. This iteration composes an initiation\\\\nphase, a procedure responsible for processing the input tokens\\\\nand generating the ﬁrst output token.
